column2: Azure SQL Database is a fully managed {{c1::platform-as-a-service (PaaS)}} database offering.
column3:
PaaS means Microsoft operates the platform and database engine for you. Application data, permissions, and object design still need your decisions.
Review source

column2: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines uses the {{c1::infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS)}} deployment model.
column3:
IaaS provides the virtual machine rather than a fully managed database. You control and maintain the guest OS and the SQL Server installation.
Review source

column2: The documented maximum storage size for a single Azure SQL Database Hyperscale database is {{c1::128 TB}}.
column3:
Storage expands as the database needs it, up to 128 TB for a single Hyperscale database. Elastic pools have a separate limit.
Review source

column2: In Azure SQL Managed Instance, In-Memory OLTP requires the {{c1::Business Critical}} service tier.
column3:
Business Critical supports memory-optimized database objects. Check the service tier when migrating a workload that depends on In-Memory OLTP.
Review source

column2: Azure SQL Managed Instance supports reliable asynchronous database messaging through {{c1::Service Broker}}.
column3:
Service Broker supports queued messages and asynchronous work. A sender can place a message in a queue rather than wait for the receiver to finish.
Review source

column2: Azure SQL Managed Instance sends email through {{c1::Database Mail}} using an external SMTP server.
column3:
Database Mail sends messages through a configured external mail relay. Configure the mail account and profile before a job can send notifications.
Review source

column2: Azure SQL Managed Instance supports {{c1::linked servers}} for accessing configured remote data sources.
column3:
A linked server defines a remote endpoint that the instance can query. Verify support for that remote source rather than assuming every SQL Server provider works.
Review source

column2: For SQL Server on Azure VMs, {{c1::Always On availability groups}} provide a database-replica-based high-availability option.
column3:
Availability groups maintain copies of databases on replicas. You design and configure failover instead of receiving all of that configuration from the VM service.
Review source

column2: For a SQL Server Azure VM, {{c1::SQL best practices assessment}} checks configuration against recommended settings.
column3:
The assessment compares instance settings with recommended practices and reports findings. It does not automatically make every suggested change.
Review source

column2: SQL database in Fabric mirrors data into OneLake as {{c1::Delta Parquet files}}.
column3:
The mirrored data is written in an analytics-friendly format. Analytical queries can read that copy instead of issuing requests against live operational tables.
Review source

column2: SQL database in Fabric replicates operational changes to OneLake in {{c1::near real time}}.
column3:
Changes appear asynchronously. A write that just committed in the operational database can take time to appear in the analytical copy.
Review source

column2: For supported cross-item queries from a Fabric SQL analytics endpoint, use {{c1::three-part names}} such as WarehouseName.dbo.TableName.
column3:
The first name identifies the other Fabric item, followed by its schema and table. Use the analytical endpoint for supported cross-item queries.
Review source

column2: Fabric source control provides {{c1::Git}} integration for SQL database development.
column3:
Git can track database object definitions and their changes. It does not record application writes as source-control commits.
Review source

column2: The Fabric portal can expose a SQL database through a {{c1::GraphQL API}}.
column3:
The API exposes selected SQL database objects to GraphQL clients. Configuration and permissions still control what an API caller can access.
Review source
